title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
event_hint: Empirical comparison of indexed semantic search and isolated deep-agent repository search
problem: Repository-level code QA requires locating relevant code scattered across many files while keeping a bounded context window. Index-based retrieval pays indexing and chunking costs, whereas delegated grep-style exploration can pollute or lose information during planner/sub-agent hand-offs; the study measures which trade-off produces accurate and affordable answers.
mechanism: Semantic Search builds a vector index over repository chunks and retrieves compact passages for a ReAct agent. Deep Agentic Search gives a planner terminal-style grep/find/glob access and delegates exploration to an isolated sub-agent that returns a condensed result, keeping raw search output out of the main context. The study compares these architectures and codes execution traces into failure modes.

evidence.claim: Semantic search answered 65.2% of SWE-QA questions correctly, versus 46.2% for deep agentic search.
evidence.condition: SWE-QA repository-level code question answering benchmark

evidence.claim: Semantic search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of deep agentic search.
evidence.baseline: Deep Agentic Search cost per correct answer

evidence.claim: The largest share of deep-agentic-search failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner/sub-agent hand-off and usually ended silently in a fluent but wrong answer.
evidence.condition: Failure taxonomy over recorded benchmark runs

evidence.claim: The compared architectures embody a trade-off: semantic search pays a one-time repository indexing cost, while deep agentic search avoids indexing but must filter raw exploration output.
evidence.condition: Repository-level code QA; vector chunks versus live terminal exploration

evidence.claim: The study reports token consumption, monetary cost, latency, effective cost per correct answer, tool usage, and trajectory length in addition to accuracy.

evaluation_context: The paper compares Semantic Search and Deep Agentic Search on the SWE-QA repository-level code QA benchmark across four language models. It analyzes recorded execution traces for tool behavior and failure modes and reports accuracy, token consumption, monetary cost, latency, and effective cost per correct answer.
limitations: The evidence here is limited to read-only repository question answering on SWE-QA and the evaluated models; it does not establish that retrieval is superior for code modification, debugging, rapidly changing repositories, or repositories whose structure is poorly indexed. Vector chunking can fragment code and miss exact dependencies, while deep search can expose native structure but remains vulnerable to hand-off omissions and context filtering. The abstract does not provide index-build latency, repository-size breakdowns, or the full accuracy/cost distribution (inference).
project_relevance: For coding-agent acceleration, a bounded task should prefer a compact, verifiable retrieval/index path when the repository can be indexed, while treating delegated exploration as a failure-prone path requiring explicit hand-off contracts and validation. The 41.8% silent hand-off failure share directly supports preserving exact task metadata, output schemas, and acceptance checks when delegating Read/Grep work (inference).
